title: No coercion (Dignitatis Humanae 2)
hook: no one may be forced to act against conscience in religious matters
tomorrow: what do you call a Christian from another church?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nostra Aetate: all peoples one community, with one origin and one final goal. One family.

Pop-ups that won't take no. A salesman with his foot in the door. The friend who keeps bringing it up until you just agree. Nobody believes a yes that was squeezed out of them. Now here's a sentence that sounds like it wandered in from the wrong book. A Church document, written by bishops who hold their faith to be true, says the right to religious freedom stays with a person even if that person isn't looking for the truth at all. Why would a Church protect the freedom of someone ignoring it?
screen: `A YES SQUEEZED OUT OF YOU.` → `A SENTENCE FROM THE WRONG BOOK?` → `FREEDOM, EVEN FOR THE ONE NOT SEEKING.`

segments.voice: The declaration is Dignitatis Humanae, of human dignity, and paragraph two solves the puzzle in three steps. First, what the freedom is. Everyone, it says, is to be free from coercion: by individuals, by social groups, by any human power at all. In religious matters, no one is to be forced to act against their conscience, or held back from acting by it, in private or in public, alone or with others, within due limits. Second, what it stands on. Not a government's permission. Not having the right answers. It stands on the dignity of the human person, known, the text says, both from God's revealed word and by reason itself. Third, why it matters. Because people are persons, with reason and free will, they're bound to seek the truth, above all religious truth, and to hold to it once they find it. And they can't do that unless they're free inside and free from pressure outside. A forced yes isn't a found truth. Now the puzzle solves itself. If the right came from seeking well, it could be lost by seeking badly. But it comes from the person. So the freedom goes wherever the person goes, even down a road the Church thinks is wrong.
screen: `FREE FROM COERCION.` · `GROUNDED IN HUMAN DIGNITY.` · `TRUTH MUST BE SOUGHT FREELY.` · `THE FREEDOM STAYS WITH THE PERSON.` · then, large: `FREE TO SEEK.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and bring to mind someone whose beliefs differ from yours, about God or about anything that matters. See them free: thinking, asking, choosing, with no one leaning on them, you included. Hold that picture with respect while the timer runs.
No coercion. Dignitatis Humanae: in religion, no one forced against conscience, because the dignity lives in the person.
Keep this: free to seek, and the freedom goes wherever the person goes. Peace till tomorrow.

chat.meaning: Dignitatis Humanae 2: no one is to be forced to act against conscience in religious matters. Truth has to be sought freely.

Dignitatis Humanae.meaning: Vatican II's declaration on religious freedom; Latin for of human dignity

coercion.meaning: forcing someone by pressure or threat

due limits.meaning: the declaration's own boundary on how the freedom is used

Nostra Aetate.meaning: Vatican II's declaration on other religions; Latin for in our time

notes: Paraphrased from DH 2: right to religious freedom; immunity from coercion by individuals, social groups and any human power; no one forced to act against conscience nor restrained from acting in accordance with it, privately or publicly, alone or with others, within due limits; based on the dignity of the person as known through revelation and reason; persons bound to seek truth, especially religious truth, and adhere to it, which requires psychological freedom and immunity from external coercion; the right continues in those who do not live up to the obligation. Confirm.
'Even down a road the Church thinks is wrong' is the script's plain-language reading of the right continuing in those who do not seek or adhere to truth; confirm.
